title: Kateri Tekakwitha
hookLine: a Mohawk and Algonquin woman who became a Christian and prayed in the woods

lines: A MOHAWK FATHER, AN ALGONQUIN MOTHER.
cards: A small cross, cut with a knife into the bark of a tree. The old accounts of her life say she made crosses like that along the paths she walked, and stopped at them to pray. No chapel.
No candles. Snow on the ground some of the year, the river close by, and a woman kneeling in the woods with a scarred face and weak eyes. Her father was Mohawk.
Her mother was Algonquin, and a Christian. The Jesuits who knew her wrote her story down. Catholics today call her a saint.

teach.h: TOLD BY THE JESUITS WHO KNEW HER.
teach.b: Her story comes to us mostly through two Jesuit priests who knew her and wrote her life. So we hear her through their eyes, and they were writing to praise her. Hold that gently.
The accounts say that as a child she survived smallpox, which left her face marked and her eyesight poor. Her parents died of the same sickness.
She grew up with relatives in a Mohawk village, and when Jesuit missionaries came, she listened. She asked for baptism and took the name Kateri, a form of Catherine.
The accounts say it cost her. Some in the village mocked her and pressured her to marry. So she left for a Christian village near Montreal, where others like her lived.
There, the accounts say, she prayed early and long, fasted hard, cared for the sick, and spent hours in the forest. She once set up a kind of woodland chapel, a cross by a stream. She died young.
Tradition says her last words were: Jesus, I love you. Her companions said that after she died, the scars on her face faded.
Mark's Gospel tells of Jesus doing much the same: "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed."
Her title, the lily of the Mohawks, came from Christians who honored her. Some Indigenous Catholics hold her close as one of their own.
Some Indigenous people remember the missions as part of a much harder story of land and loss.
Both memories are real, and her life sits inside both.

how: Catholics in the United States and Canada visit shrines connected with Kateri Tekakwitha and ask her prayers, and some Indigenous Catholic communities keep her feast day with their own songs and customs.

games.q: you're a young Mohawk woman, newly baptized. some in your village mock you and press you to marry. what do you do?
o: give up the new faith to keep the peace.
leave for a Christian village where others pray as you do.
stay, and hide your faith completely.
games.why: the accounts say she left for a Christian village near Montreal, where she prayed, fasted, cared for the sick, and set up a cross by a stream in the forest.

practice: Step outside if you can, or open a window wide, and find one living thing, a tree, a patch of grass, a weed in a crack, to be your marker, the way her crosses in bark were hers. Be still with it.
If you pray, pray there in your own words or with the Lord's Prayer; if you don't, just listen to whatever is outside.

wordCard.voice: Kateri Tekakwitha. A Mohawk and Algonquin woman who was baptized, left home for a Christian village, and prayed in the woods. Catholics honor her as a saint.

carryVoice: Your line: the lily of the Mohawks. Prayer in the woods, by a cross in the bark. See you tomorrow.
